'''Charles Nohuoma Rotimi''' (born 1957) is the Scientific Director of the [[National Human Genome Research Institute]] (NHGRI).<ref name="NIH Intramural Research Program 2021 j885">{{cite web | title=Charles Rotimi, Ph.D., Is NHGRI's New Scientific Director | website=NIH Intramural Research Program | date=2021-10-10 | url=https://irp.nih.gov/catalyst/29/6/charles-rotimi-phd-is-nhgris-new-scientific-director | access-date=2023-08-09}}</ref>
He joined the [[National Institutes of Health]] (NIH) in 2008 as the inaugural Director of the Trans-NIH{{refn|group=lower-alpha|"Trans" as in "Trans-National"}} Center for Research in [[Genomics]] and [[Global health|Global Health]] and was also the chief of the NHGRI's Metabolic, Cardiovascular, and Inflammatory Disease Genomics Branch. He works to ensure that [[population genetics]] include genomes from African populations and founded the [[African Society of Human Genetics]] in 2003 and was elected its first president. Rotimi was instrumental in the launch of the [[Human Heredity and Health in Africa]] (H3Africa) with the NIH and the [[Wellcome Trust]]. He was elected to the [[National Academy of Medicine]] in 2018.
== Early life and education ==
Rotimi was born in [[Benin City]], [[Nigeria]], and is the second oldest of six children.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.the-scientist.com/profile/charles-rotimi-works-to-ensure-genetic-epidemiology-and-population-genetics-studies-include-dna-from-africannot-just-europeanpopulations--64818|title=Genome Collector: A Profile of Charles Rotimi|website=The Scientist Magazine|language=en|access-date=2019-05-08}}</ref> His mother had no education and his father was a high school English teacher.<ref name=":0" /> Rotimi studied at the [[University of Benin (Nigeria)|University of Benin]] and graduated in 1979.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Morris|first=Kelly|date=2010-10-23|title=Charles Rotimi: engaging Africa in human genomic research|journal=The Lancet|language=English|volume=376|issue=9750|pages=1383|doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(10)61943-5|issn=0140-6736|pmid=20971351|s2cid=8083562|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.genome.gov/staff/Charles-N-Rotimi-PhD|title=Charles N. Rotimi, Ph.D. |publisher= NHGRI|website=genome.gov|access-date=2019-05-08}}</ref> He led the chemistry lab at a high school in [[Benin]].<ref name=":0" /> He decided to attend graduate school abroad, and applied to universities in the [[United Kingdom]] and [[United States]].<ref name=":0" /> He was supported by his family to attend the [[University of Mississippi]], where he studied [[Health administration|health care administration]].<ref name=":0" /> He flew from [[Nigeria]] to [[Mississippi]] via [[London]], including catching a helicopter from [[Gatwick Airport]] to [[Heathrow Airport]].<ref name=":0" /> While studying at the [[University of Mississippi]], Rotimi met his wife Deatrice, who was from [[Chicago]]. He graduated with a [[master's degree]] in 1983.<ref name=":0" /> In 1985 he returned to [[Nigeria]] and was appointed an administrator at a local health ministry. He returned to America to complete a program in [[epidemiology]] at the [[University of Alabama]], and was awarded a full scholarship to complete a doctorate.<ref name=":0" /> Rotimi completed his PhD and then spent a year as a postdoc at the [[Loma Linda University]] in [[California]]. Here he worked on [[Alzheimer's disease]].<ref name=":0" />

== Research and career ==
Rotimi investigates genetics and [[health disparities]], ensuring that African genomes are represented in genome databases.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Cooper|first1=R|last2=Rotimi|first2=C|last3=Ataman|first3=S|last4=McGee|first4=D|last5=Osotimehin|first5=B|last6=Kadiri|first6=S|last7=Muna|first7=W|last8=Kingue|first8=S|last9=Fraser|first9=H|date=February 1997|title=The prevalence of hypertension in seven populations of west African origin|journal=American Journal of Public Health|volume=87|issue=2|pages=160–168|issn=0090-0036|pmc=1380786|pmid=9103091|doi=10.2105/ajph.87.2.160}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.newsweek.com/2018/07/27/cancer-cure-genome-cancer-treatment-africa-genetic-charles-rotimi-dna-human-1024630.html|title=Cancer scientists have ignored African DNA in the search for cures|last=EDT|first=Jessica Wapner On 7/18/18 at 9:01 AM|date=2018-07-18|website=Newsweek|language=en-US|access-date=2019-05-09}}</ref> He was appointed as an [[Epidemiology|epidemiologist]] at [[Loyola University Chicago]], where he worked on [[cardiovascular disease]] and [[obesity]] in people in the [[African diaspora]].<ref name=":0" /> Together with his colleague [[Richard S. Cooper|Richard Cooper]], Rotimi recruited 10,000 people to study the prevalence of [[hypertension]] in populations of West African descent.<ref name=":2" /> He found that hypertension and diabetes rates are significantly higher in African-American populations in [[Chicago]] than they are in rural Africa. He attributed this to lifestyle factors, including weight, salt consumption and levels of physical activity.<ref name=":2" />

Rotimi moved to [[Howard University]] in 1990, where he worked with [[Georgia M. Dunston]] at the National Human Genome Center. Rotimi was promoted{{when|date=May 2019}} to head of genetic [[epidemiology]].<ref name=":0" /> Here he studied the impact of the underrepresentation of African and African-American data in genomic datasets.<ref name=":0" /> He argued for the use of genomic tools to understand variation in human biology, but pointed out that it is not possible to use genetics to define race; the variation in genomes do not account for the socially defined racial groups and racial self-identity.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Rotimi|first=Charles N.|date=2004-10-26|title=Are medical and nonmedical uses of large-scale genomic markers conflating genetics and 'race'?|journal=Nature Genetics|language=en|volume=36|issue=11s|pages=S43–S47|doi=10.1038/ng1439|pmid=15508002|issn=1546-1718|doi-access=free}} {{closed access}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Keita|first1=S. O. Y.|last2=Kittles|first2=R. A.|last3=Royal|first3=C. D. M.|last4=Bonney|first4=G. E.|last5=Furbert-Harris|first5=P.|last6=Dunston|first6=G. M.|last7=Rotimi|first7=C. N.|date=2004|title=Conceptualizing human variation|journal=Nature Genetics|volume=36|issue=11 Suppl|pages=S17–20|doi=10.1038/ng1455|issn=1061-4036|pmid=15507998|doi-access=free}} {{closed access}}</ref> He compiled genomic data from 6,000 people in 13 language families, identifying 21 global genetic ancestries.<ref name=":0" /> The study established that 97 % of people have mixed ancestry, emphasising the problems with labels such as [[hispanic]], [[Black people|black]] and [[White people|white]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Shriner|first1=Daniel|last2=Rotimi|first2=Charles N.|last3=Baker|first3=Jennifer L.|date=2017-05-08|title=Human ancestry correlates with language and reveals that race is not an objective genomic classifier|journal=Scientific Reports|language=en|volume=7|issue=1|pages=1572|doi=10.1038/s41598-017-01837-7|doi-access=free|pmid=28484253|pmc=5431528|issn=2045-2322|bibcode=2017NatSR...7.1572B}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lawrence|first=David|date=2004-11-20|title=A rational basis for race|journal=The Lancet|language=English|volume=364|issue=9448|pages=1845–1846|doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(04)17459-X|issn=0140-6736|pmid=15565745|s2cid=42384457|doi-access=free}}</ref> In an interview with ''[[The Lancet]]'', Rotimi described inequality as "one of the most outrageous aspects of society".<ref name=":1" />

Rotimi led the African component of the [[International HapMap Project]], which contributed to the [[1000 Genomes Project]].<ref name=":0" /> He recruited three African communities in [[Kenya]] and [[Nigeria]], ensuring that African genomes were part of the record.<ref name=":0" /> It is understood that [[homo sapiens]] originated in Africa, leaving after 100,000 years.<ref name=":0" /> During this time much of the [[genetic evolution]] had already occurred, and those that emigrated carried a subset of the original genetic diversity. African genomes are the most ancient.<ref name=":0" /> 

Rotimi looks at the [[heritability]] of complex disease.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Visscher|first1=Peter M.|last2=McCarroll|first2=Steven A.|last3=Mackay|first3=Trudy F. C.|last4=Haines|first4=Jonathan L.|last5=Gibson|first5=Greg|last6=Eichler|first6=Evan E.|last7=Clark|first7=Andrew G.|last8=Boehnke|first8=Michael|last9=Whittemore|first9=Alice S.|date=2009|title=Finding the missing heritability of complex diseases|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=461|issue=7265|pages=747–753|doi=10.1038/nature08494|pmid=19812666|issn=1476-4687|pmc=2831613|bibcode=2009Natur.461..747M}}</ref> He began to work with [[Kári Stefánsson]] in 2007, studying the diabetes risk variant [[TCF7L2]] in West African populations.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Stefánsson|first1=Kári|last2=Rotimi|first2=Charles|last3=Kong|first3=Augustine|last4=Gulcher|first4=Jeffrey R.|last5=Thorsteinsdottir|first5=Unnur|last6=Pedersen|first6=Oluf|last7=Hebebrand|first7=Johannes|last8=Sigurdsson|first8=Gunnar|last9=Christiansen|first9=Claus|date=2007|title=Refining the impact of TCF7L2 gene variants on type 2 diabetes and adaptive evolution|journal=Nature Genetics|language=en|volume=39|issue=2|pages=218–225|doi=10.1038/ng1960|pmid=17206141|s2cid=10529476|issn=1546-1718}}</ref> He demonstrated that both [[TCF7L2]] and its genetic variant HapA increase the risk of diabetes due to their function in energy [[metabolism]]. To determine the origins of the [[sickle cell disease]] mutation, Rotimi studied the genomes of 3,000 people.<ref name=":0" /> He identified that [[Sickle cell disease|sickle cell]] emerged around 7,000 years ago in [[Africa]].<ref name=":0" />

Rotimi joined the [[National Institutes of Health]] in 2007, where he became founding director of the Trans-NIH Center for Research on Genomics and Global Health.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://irp.nih.gov/pi/charles-rotimi|title=Principal Investigators|website=NIH Intramural Research Program|language=en|access-date=2019-05-08}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.genome.gov/about-nhgri/Center-for-Research-on-Genomics-and-Global-Health|title=Center for Research on Genomics and Global Health {{!}} NHGRI|website=genome.gov|access-date=2019-05-08}}</ref> He works with [[Francis Collins]] on making genomic studies more inclusive.<ref name=":0" /> Rotimi founded the [[African Society of Human Genetics]] in 2003.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.afshg.org/about/|title=About – AfSHG – African Society of Human Genetics|language=en-US|access-date=2019-05-08}}</ref> He launched the Human Heredity and Health in Africa (H3Africa) initiative with the African Society of Human Genetics, a $70 million collaboration between the [[National Institutes of Health]] and [[Wellcome Trust]].<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.afshg.org/h3africa/|title=Human Heredity and Health in Africa (H3Africa) – AfSHG – African Society of Human Genetics|language=en-US|access-date=2019-05-08}}</ref> He described the project as a "lifetime achievement".<ref name=":1" />

===Awards and honors===
Rotimi was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Medicine]] (NAM) in 2018.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nam.edu/national-academy-of-medicine-elects-85-new-members/|title=National Academy of Medicine Elects 85 New Members|date=2018-10-15|website=nam.edu|publisher=National Academy of Medicine|language=en-US|access-date=2019-05-08}}</ref> He serves on the editorial boards of ''[[Public Health Genomics (journal)|Public Health Genomics]]'', ''[[Genome Medicine]]'', ''[[Clinical Genetics (journal)|Clinical Genetics]]'' and the ''Journal of Applied and Translational Genomics''.<ref name=":3" /> He was awarded the [[Curt Stern Award]] from the [[American Society of Human Genetics]] in 2019 for his contributions to genetics in African and African-descent populations.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.ashg.org/press/201907-Curt-Stern-Award.shtml|title=ASHG Honors Charles Rotimi & Sarah Tishkoff with 2019 Curt Stern Award {{!}} ASHG|website=www.ashg.org|date=22 July 2019|language=en|access-date=2019-07-25}}</ref>
